'''''Prunus domestica''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Rosaceae]]. A [[deciduous]] tree, it includes many varieties of the fruit trees known as [[plum]]s in English, though not all plums belong to this species. The [[greengage]]s and [[damson]]s also belong to subspecies of ''P. domestica''.

==Description==

It typically forms a large [[shrub]] or a small tree. It may be somewhat thorny, with white blossom, borne in early spring. The oval or spherical fruit varies in size, but can be up to {{Convert|8|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} across. The pulp is usually sweet,<ref name="GYOF">{{cite book |last=Klein |first=Carol |url=https://archive.org/details/growyourownfruit0000klei_w4b3/page/96/ |title=Grow Your Own Fruit |publisher=[[Mitchell Beazley]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-84533-4345 |location=United Kingdom |pages=96–97}}</ref> but some [[Variety (botany)|varieties]] are sour. Like all ''Prunus'' fruits, it contains a single large seed, usually called a stone, which is discarded when eating.

==Taxonomy==
The species' [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] parentage was believed to be ''[[Prunus spinosa]]'' and ''[[Prunus cerasifera|P. cerasifera]]'';<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Crane |first1=M.B. |url=http://krishikosh.egranth.ac.in/bitstream/1/2045588/1/16908.pdf |title=The Genetics of Garden Plants |last2=Lawrence |first2=W.J.C. |publisher=MacMillan & Co. LTD |year=1947 |page=233 |access-date=2017-06-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171215084723/http://krishikosh.egranth.ac.in/bitstream/1/2045588/1/16908.pdf |archive-date=2017-12-15 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Khanizadeh, S. |title=Our Plums/Les Pruniers de chez nous |author2=Cousineau, J. |publisher=Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada/Agriculteur et Agroalimentaire Canada |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-660-61568-4}}</ref> however, recent cytogenetic evidence seem to implicate 2×, 4×, 6×{{efn|Diploid, tetraploid, hexaploid: see [[Polyploidy#Polyploid types|Polyploidy]]}} ''P. cerasifera'' as the sole wild stock from which the cultivated 6× ''P. domestica'' could have evolved.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zohary |first=Daniel |date=1992-03-01 |title=Is the European plum, Prunus domestica L., a P. cerasifera EHRH. × P. spinosa L. allo-polyploid? |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00022260 |journal=Euphytica |language=en |volume=60 |issue=1 |pages=75–77 |doi=10.1007/BF00022260 |bibcode=1992Euphy..60...75Z |issn=0014-2336 |s2cid=10923512|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Subspecies ===
Cullen ''et al.'' (1995) recognises three subspecies,<ref>Cullen, J. et al. (1995). [https://books.google.com/books?id=Ly7ESAAACAAJ ''The European Garden Flora. Volume IV'']. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge.</ref> though scientific studies<!-- see e.g. "Ripening Time, Quality and Resistance Donors of Genotypes of Prunus domestica" -->{{Which|date = August 2022|reason = Need a proper ref not a hidden comment.}} favor a more fine-grained separation:
{|
|
* ''P. domestica'' ssp. ''domestica'' – [[prune plum]]s, [[zwetschge]] (including ssp. ''oeconomica''<!-- Borkh., nom. illeg. -->)
* ''P. domestica'' ssp. ''insititia'' – [[damson]]s and [[bullace]]s, ''krieche'', ''kroosjes'', [[perdrigon]] and other European varieties
* ''P. domestica'' ssp. ''intermedia'' – [[egg plum]]s (including [[Victoria plum]])
* ''P. domestica'' ssp. ''italica'' – gages ([[greengage]]s, [[round plum]]s etc.; including sspp. ''claudiana'' and ''rotunda'')
* ''P. domestica'' ssp. ''pomariorum'' – spilling
* ''P. domestica'' ssp. ''prisca'' – [[zibarte]]
* ''P. domestica'' ssp. ''syriaca'' – [[mirabelle plum]]s
|}
The subspecies cross easily, so that numerous intermediate forms can be found: their sweetness and tartness may vary, their colors varying from bluish-purple to red, orange, yellow or light green.{{cn|date=August 2024}}

==Uses==

The pulp is edible<ref>{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Eastern Region |publisher=Knopf |year=1980 |isbn=0-394-50760-6 |location=New York |page=498}}</ref> and usually sweet, though some varieties are sour and require cooking with sugar to make them palatable.

[[Plum]]s are grown commercially in orchards, but modern [[rootstock]]s, together with self-fertile strains, training and pruning methods, allow single plums to be grown in relatively small spaces. Their early flowering and fruiting means that they require a sheltered spot away from frosts and cold winds.<ref name="GYOF" />

Most [[prune]]s (dried plums) are made from fruits of this species.{{cn|date=August 2024}}
